query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A specifically designed phase‐selective recrystallization heat treatment will simultaneously increase both the strength and ductility of a eutectic high-entropy alloy by transforming its initial coarse lamellar structure into a dual-phase microstructure with a recrystallized soft phase embedded in a hard phase skeleton.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a coarse, lamellar microstructure with distinct soft and hard phases, where the soft phase has limited work hardening due to weak phase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Application of a controlled heat treatment (phase-selective recrystallization) that selectively recrystallizes the soft phase without substantially altering the hard phase.
generation.conditions: Processing of pre-deformed eutectic high-entropy alloy under optimized annealing temperatures (below the melting point of the hard phase) and durations that promote recrystallization only in the soft phase, ensuring favorable strain partitioning.
generation.structural_mediator: A dual-phase microstructure consisting of a fully recrystallized, fine-grained soft phase embedded within an interconnected hard phase skeleton.
generation.mechanism: The treatment eliminates weak boundaries in the soft phase and enhances strain compatibility between phases. The recrystallized soft phase exhibits improved work hardening, while the hard phase provides reinforcement, together leading to a synergistic improvement in both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated eutectic alloy, the treated material is expected to exhibit significantly increased ultimate tensile strength (approaching ~2 GPa) and enhanced uniform elongation (around 35%), though precise increments may vary with processing parameters.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated eutectic high-entropy alloy with its coarse lamellar structure and limited ductility under conventional processing routes.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention is anticipated in eutectic high-entropy alloys where well-differentiated soft and hard phases are present; results may not be directly applicable to alloys lacking such phase distinctions or requiring different processing histories.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal annealing temperature, time, and pre-deformation conditions are not fully established and may need fine-tuning for different alloy compositions. The precise magnitude of improvements in mechanical properties could vary based on these parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple samples of the eutectic high-entropy alloy with identical initial microstructures. Subject them to a series of phase-selective recrystallization heat treatments varying in temperature and duration. Use tensile testing and detailed microstructural characterization (e.g., EBSD and TEM) to compare the mechanical properties and phase distributions of treated samples against untreated controls.
measurements: Phase distribution and grain size via EBSD/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If none of the heat treatment conditions results in a simultaneous and statistically significant improvement in both strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if the resulting microstructure does not display the predicted dual-phase architecture, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Phase-selective recrystallization makes eutectic high-entropy alloys ultra-ductile

Abstract: Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa.
